hints.title: Make a column for each position
hints.body: Write the three rejected passwords underneath each other. Cross out, in each column, all the letters already tried there.
hints.recap: A zero score rules out each tried letter in its particular position.
hints.pitfall: Every letter is still used somewhere in the password.
hints.pause: List the letters still allowed in each position.

recall.reminder: A zero score rules out each tried letter in its particular position.

hints.title: List full passwords that still fit
hints.body: Combine the allowed letters into complete passwords, using each letter exactly once. Keep only strings that meet all three zero-score restrictions.
hints.recap: Every candidate must satisfy all the restrictions at once.
hints.pitfall: Choosing letters independently can repeat one letter and miss another.

recall.reminder: Every candidate must satisfy all the restrictions at once.

hints.title: Compare the possible feedback
hints.body: Try one of your remaining strings as the next guess. Count how many positions it would match against each possible password. Different feedback totals let you tell those passwords apart.
hints.recap: A strategy works only if every possible true password can be identified.
hints.pitfall: You need to deduce the password, not necessarily type it correctly.
hints.pause: Check whether the feedback distinguishes all cases, and justify the least number of further trials.

recall.reminder: A strategy works only if every possible true password can be identified.

solution:
The possibilities are bcead, beacd, dceab and deacb. A trial of bcead returns respectively 5, 2, 3 and 0 correctly positioned letters.

Because these four responses are distinct, one further trial tells us which of the four passwords is correct. Zero further trials cannot suffice because all four are still possible beforehand. Answer B.
knowledgePattern: Design one query whose response distinguishes all remaining permutations
